executiveSummary: Port Alder, a Maine fishing town of 1,900, lost power for eleven days in 2023. Instead of waiting, its residents raised $2.1M, fought the utility and an ice storm, and built a community microgrid that cut outage hours from 286 to 2. The lesson: resilience is built by neighbors, and any town can start with twelve people and one roof.

slides.slideTitle: The town that learned to keep its own lights on
slides.subtitle: Port Alder, Maine · A story about resilience
slides.visualDescription: A small harbor town at blue hour, lobster boats at their moorings, a few windows lit
slides.speakerNotes:
- Good morning. I want to tell you about a fishing town of 1,900 people.
- Nothing about Port Alder is special. That's the point.
- By the end, I hope you'll want to go home and do what they did.
slides.purpose: Opens the story in a quiet, ordinary place
slides.intent: Make the audience settle in for a story

slides.slideTitle: For eleven days in October, Port Alder went dark
keyBullets: 11 days
without power after Storm Elsa, October 2023
slides.visualDescription: A dark harbor at night, one lantern on a dock, storm clouds overhead
slides.speakerNotes:
- On October 9th, 2023, Storm Elsa took down the only transmission line into town.
- It was eleven days before power came back.
- The co-op's freezers failed on day two. Forty thousand pounds of lobster spoiled.
- Two elderly residents were hospitalized from the cold.
slides.purpose: Delivers the crisis as one stark number
slides.intent: Make the audience feel the shock of the outage

slides.slideTitle: Waiting for permission was the real outage
keyBullets: We weren't waiting for the grid. We were waiting for someone to tell us we were allowed to fix it.
Ruth Calloway, harbor master, Port Alder
slides.visualDescription: Portrait of a weathered harbor master in a kitchen, morning light, coffee mug
slides.speakerNotes: Ruth said this to me in her kitchen, a year after the storm. The town had the people, the roofs, and the will. What it didn't have was anyone telling it that a town could build its own power. That sentence is the hinge of this whole story.
slides.purpose: Names the real obstacle in a resident's words
slides.intent: Make the audience feel the frustration of waiting

slides.slideTitle: So the town decided to build its own grid
slides.subtitle: Three hundred households, one fishing co-op, and no experience at all
slides.speakerNotes:
- In January 2024, sixty people packed the grange hall.
- Nobody there had built anything bigger than a boat shed.
- They voted 58 to 2 to try.
slides.intent: Make the audience root for the town

slides.slideTitle: How a town talked itself into a power plant
keyBullets: Spring 2024: knock on every door / will anyone sign up? / hopeful but unsure
Summer 2024: raise $2.1M from 312 households and a state grant / this might actually work / proud
Winter 2024: bolt the first panels to the co-op roof / we did this ourselves / elated
slides.speakerNotes:
- The first phase was door-knocking. Twelve volunteers visited every house.
- By summer, 312 households had pledged, and a state resilience grant matched them.
- In December, the first panels went up on the co-op roof in a snowstorm.
slides.purpose: Shows the journey's first stretch and how it felt
slides.intent: Make the audience feel the town's momentum

slides.slideTitle: Twice in one year, the project nearly died
keyBullets: Jan 2025: the utility denies the interconnection permit
Mar 2025: an ice storm cracks the first battery enclosure
Jun 2025: a court rules the co-op may sell power to its members
Sep 2025: the microgrid passes its first islanding test
slides.speakerNotes:
- January: the utility said no. Their lawyers said a fishing co-op couldn't be a power company.
- March: an ice storm cracked a battery enclosure and we lost two months.
- June: the state court sided with the town.
- September: we cut the line to the grid on purpose, and the lights stayed on.
slides.intent: Make the audience feel the struggle was real

slides.slideTitle: The ice storm left them $412,000 over budget
keyBullets: over budget, covered by 140 neighbors in nine days
slides.visualDescription: A glass jar of bills on a general store counter, handwritten sign
slides.speakerNotes:
- When the enclosure cracked, the project was $412,000 short.
- The bank said no. The state said wait.
- So the co-op put a jar on the counter at the general store, and 140 neighbors covered it in nine days.
- That's the moment I knew this would work.
slides.purpose: Shows the low point and the community's answer
slides.intent: Make the audience feel the cost and the courage

slides.slideTitle: From diesel on every dock to sun and storage
keyBullets: Before: 31 hours of outages a year, and a diesel generator on every dock
After: 2 hours of outages a year, with the harbor running on sun and storage
slides.speakerNotes:
- Before the microgrid, the harbor ran on hope and diesel.
- Today, the batteries carry the harbor through anything short of a direct hit.
- The generators are still there. Nobody has started one in a year.
slides.purpose: Shows the change in one side-by-side
slides.intent: Make the audience feel the transformation

slides.slideTitle: Outage hours fell from 286 to 2 in three years
slides.subtitle: Hours without power per year, Port Alder
keyBullets: Outage hours fell to 2 in 2026, after 286 in the storm year
slides.speakerNotes:
- This is the chart I show every town council.
- 2023 is the spike: the storm.
- Since the microgrid came online, outages have all but disappeared.
slides.intent: Make the audience believe the result is real

slides.slideTitle: What the town got back was more than electricity
keyBullets: 62%: of electricity now made in town
$340: saved per household each year
0: hours dark during Storm Nadia, 2026
14: towns that have asked for the playbook
slides.speakerNotes:
- 62% of the town's power is now made in town.
- Households save $340 a year on average.
- When Storm Nadia hit in August, Port Alder was the only lit town on the peninsula.
- And fourteen other towns have called asking how.
slides.intent: Make the audience feel the payoff

slides.slideTitle: Resilience is built by neighbors, not delivered to them
slides.subtitle: Every town has the people; few have been told they're allowed to start
slides.speakerNotes:
- This is what I came here to say.
- We talk about resilience as infrastructure: wires, poles, substations.
- But in Port Alder, resilience was neighbors who had done something hard together and knew they could again.
slides.purpose: States the lesson of the story
slides.intent: Make the audience adopt the idea as their own

slides.slideTitle: How your town can start next month
keyBullets: Map: list the buildings that must never go dark
Gather: find the twelve people who will knock on doors
Ask: request the interconnection study before you need it
Build: start with one roof and one battery
slides.speakerNotes:
- Four steps. None of them needs an engineer.
- Start with the list: the clinic, the school, the store with the freezers.
- Then find your twelve. Every town has them.
- Ask for the study early; it takes a year.
slides.purpose: Gives the audience a concrete starting path
slides.intent: Make the audience feel they can do this too

slides.slideTitle: Go home and find your twelve people
slides.subtitle: portalderpower.org/playbook
slides.visualDescription: The harbor at dawn, every window lit, boats heading out
slides.speakerNotes:
- Port Alder didn't have money, expertise, or permission.
- It had twelve people willing to knock on doors.
- Go home and find yours. The playbook is free. Thank you.
slides.purpose: Ends on a clear, personal call to action
slides.intent: Make the audience leave determined to act
